utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we come to the subject matter of your testimony, may we please hear your name, your first name and if so, your nickname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Petar Stanar, nicknamed Cile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 13th of September, 1954, Maricka Municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And your current place of residence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still the same place, Omarska without number, Omarska. I have been living there all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For procedural reasons, are you in any way relative to the accused in this case, to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are the sons of two sisters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise. Who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are children of two sisters of first blood. So we are first cousins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This we'll say, it's always extremely difficult to find out these linear or collateral relations. Your mother and the mother of Dr. Stakic, they are sisters. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then before we start with the testimony, I have to go into some legal details and ask the parties for their submissions on this. Our rules on procedure and evidence don't have any rules on the right to refuse testimony on personal grounds. Nevertheless, a comparative approach seems to give the impression that in a number of countries, the following persons may refuse to testify: The fiance of the accused, the spouse of the accused, even if the marriage no longer exists, a person who is linearly related or related by marriage, collaterally related to the third degree, or related by marriage to the second degree to the accused. This seems to be what some legal systems have in common. But I can't see that the current relationship just demonstrated by the witness grants a right to refuse testimony on personal grounds. Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In all legal systems of the former Yugoslavia, it would be the ground to refuse the testimony actually. Even further relation, collateral relation would be grounds to refuse the testimony, but we never spoke with this witness so we don't know what is his standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest that we find out if it's theoretical or a real issue, but our submission is that given the importance of cases at this Tribunal and the lack of any privilege stated in the rules, that the witnesses would not have privilege, certainly not a cousin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the logical order is first to find out what are the prerequisites, and then to ask the witness. May I ask you, Mr. Stanar, do you want, if there would be - and I emphasise "if there would be" - an obstacle by your relation -- based on your relationship to Dr. Stakic to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see no reason for any obstacle. I can answer the questions that you have to put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a practical solution. Then we can continue. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we please hear in context your professional career starting at that point of time when you were, as I assume, gainfully employed in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, before I started to work in the Municipality of Prijedor in 1990, I worked as a driver in Ljubljana, and I was there for 18 years. And when the division came about, I was fired in Ljubljana by my company because I was a Serb, and that was when I returned. And then I spent a year on the waiting list, on a laid-off list. And since I was a professional driver, I applied at the employment bureau, and the municipality gave me the job of a driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And do you recall the exact date when was it that you were gainfully employed in the municipality as a driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started working there on the 17th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you still employed by the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and I'm still the driver of the President Muharem Murselovic, the current president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I ask, was there a pool of drivers in the Municipal Assembly, or were you assigned to drive a special car, or were you assigned to drive a special person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were five of us, and we all worked together. As the need arose, we would be issued the order and drive wherever, and we are still five, and we work based on the same principles as we did in 1992, that is, we are issued the order to drive wherever is necessary, and we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe my question was not concrete enough. Were you assigned, for example -- or as you told us, at the moment you are driving the current president of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality of Prijedor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In 1992, were you the driver of a concrete person, say also at that time the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The then-president, Milomir Stakic, didn't have a driver of his own. He would ask any of our four, five drivers to take him wherever. And since I lived in Omarska and he lived in Omarska, he would usually call me so if we could go back home. But to drive around for business, he would ask for any of the drivers because there was nobody assigned to him, nobody was there to wait for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have special log books, either related to a certain person or to a certain car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing specific. I had a Jetta, a 12-year-old car that I was issued with first. And I started working there with that car. I didn't have any particular instructions or any particular logbooks. We worked regularly just as we work now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When arriving, just that we have an impression of your working day, would you go in the morning first to the building of the municipality and wait there for instructions? Or was it already the day before that you got the instructions "Tomorrow you have to drive Mr. X or Y"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would happen in the morning. We get to work. And they'd tell me the boss is calling you. It was Zeljko Grahovac who was my boss. He gives me several orders, as well you are supposed to go to such and such place. He gives you the order, and we're off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So coming back to 1992, who was at that time your superior, your immediate superior in the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Zeljko Grahovac, because I was a driver, so I was under him. But he must have been receiving his orders and tasks from somebody who was above him. But my orders were issued by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And could you please tell us who was the superior to Zeljko Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I guess the president or the secretary, one of those two. Just as it is today. But nothing special. Now, my boss is Zoran and at that time it was Zeljko Grahovac. And who was his superior, well, it was either the secretary or the president. I don't know. I don't know who it is today either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us that you started your work the 17th of May, 1992. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The other day, I found this decision, and I saw it was the 17th of May. That day, I was issued the decision for a trial work for a month. That is, if I proved to be up to the task, then they would decide whether I would be taken on permanently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you by chance have this document with you, this decision you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I left it at home. I didn't bring it with me. I have it in a drawer, and I could have taken it. I simply forgot it, but there was this document, it says the 17th of May, and I can now prove it and document it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So my understanding from your testimony is that there was nothing like a logbook in the cars. And how was your work controlled? Did you have to sign in in the morning and sign out in the evening, or how did it work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, we got to our workplace. We sit down. As we are sitting now in the janitor's room, that is where we could sit. And we sit there and wait for our assignments. There was no logbook kept, but it was natural for us to get to work at 7.00, and then to wait for assignments except when we have to go further away, to Banja Luka or some other place, then we would know it in advance. But otherwise, we are issued with the travel order that says "Municipality of Prijedor." It covers our area, and you just drive around with that travel order which can be valid for a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many drivers and how many cars were available in 1992? On the channel 4, I just listened B/C/S and not English. Could this please be changed. Can we continue? Okay. So the question was how many drivers and how many cars were available in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I joined in 1992, there were five drivers, me, Dragomir Grandic. This was this man called Bogunovic. Let me try and remember his first name. There was a man called Miro, and a man called Ergelic. There were five of us when I worked there. There were five of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many cars and please, which kind of cars? Golf? Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one Mercedes, one Jetta that I drove, and there were three Lada cars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How often did you drive the president of the Municipal Assembly at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be the one who would drive him from home and back home. And I would take him in my Jetta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What period of time, that would from as from the 17th of May until what is important here, September/October 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, up to then. It was either in September or October that I worked there. And after that, I was mobilised and I was sent to the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where lived Dr. Stakic at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period of time, he lived in Omarska. He lived in Omarska, and his landlady was -- I don't remember her name. That's where he lived, in Omarska. I really don't know the name of these two ladies in whose house he resided, but there were two ladies. He was their tenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't he live together with his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His family was living with him in rented accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And without any doubt, it's your testimony as you sit here that you brought on a daily basis Dr. Stakic in the morning from Omarska and in the evening back to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to the 30th of April, the 1st of May, I would drive him regularly. After the 1st of May, we didn't go there any longer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then maybe it was my fault. So please, once again maybe I was misled, did you before you received the final decision that you would drive for the or on behalf of the Municipal Assembly a period of time already beforehand? Because previously you mentioned that you found a decision starting your work the 17th of May. And now you're discussing the 30th of April and the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not April. I started in May, so it must have been June. I made a mistake. It was June. May, June, up to June, yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it can help you, do you recall the so-called takeover of Prijedor which happened, in fact, as you indicated, on the 30th of April to the 1st of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I didn't work at that time. I started working later than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But why did you mention on line 9 -- line 21 page 9 of today's transcript, "That up to the 30th of April, the 1st of May, I would drive him regularly? After the 1st of May, we didn't go there any longer," which in fact would be in line with other testimonies we heard here in this courtroom before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of the attack on Prijedor, and after that, we didn't go there any longer. I don't know when that happened, whether it was on the 30th or -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you remember the takeover of Prijedor, which was I think for all citizens of Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I don't remember the takeover in Prijedor. I wasn't there. I started working when the president of the Municipal Assembly was Stakic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I think it's in the moment - the parties may correct me if I'm wrong - undisputed among the parties that Dr. Stakic became the president of the Municipal Assembly the 30th of April, 1992, already. So could you please try to recall when it was now exactly that for the first time you drove Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Starting with the 17th of April, that is, the 17th of May, when I started working, I started taking him to Omarska. I would go home and he would come with me. Up to the attack on Prijedor, and then things changed after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry that I don't understand. It reads now: "Starting with the 17th of April, that is, the 17th of May." When did you actually start? Maybe one explanation could be that, in fact, that you got the work the 17th of May, and there was a, call it, test period before you got the final decision that you were gainfully employed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it says that on the 17th of May, I was given this decision to start working as a driver in the municipality of Prijedor, and I started driving after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you maybe, without being a driver in the municipality of Prijedor, on a private or semi-private basis drive Dr. Stakic from Omarska to Prijedor and the way back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't drive him in my private car. I would drive him in the official car. And when we went home, we went home together to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever drive him in his private car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So when you drove Dr. Stakic, did you call -- did you get a call by the secretary or by your direct superior asking "Please, Dr. Stakic needs a car today and please take the one" -- I think you mentioned it was a Jetta --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then it would be the decision of Dr. Stakic where to go? Or did you already know beforehand what would be the final destination of your ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be given an order to drive, and I would drive wherever President Stakic told me to go. I would go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So can you please tell us what were the main destinations where you travelled to with Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all over Prijedor, he would visit all sorts of institutions, schools, companies, electrical board, medical institutions. He was in charge of all of these institutions, and he would visit them very often. Sometimes he would go to Banja Luka to the municipality. He went everywhere. He was always on the move. And when he didn't go anywhere, he would receive people in his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned he would visit all sorts of institutions. Did he, for example, visit the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't go to Ljubija because the main office of the Ljubija mine is very close to the municipal building. If he went there, he would go on foot. There was no need for me to drive him there. This office was the main office for the Ljubija mine, and it was behind the municipal building in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We know. Could you give us some examples of places Dr. Stakic would have visited at that time in the entire municipality of Prijedor. Hamlets, small towns, institutions there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't go to these little hamlets. If he went anywhere, he would go to the municipal building in Banja Luka or elsewhere where they needed him. In Prijedor, he visited all sorts of companies, the railway, Zitopromet, Kozaraputevi, public utilities, all such institutions which had problems then as they have them now. He would very often go to the hospital. All sorts of places he would visit. We didn't go to any of the smaller hamlets. There was no need for him to go there. If he went anywhere from outside Prijedor, he would go to Banja Luka mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So whom would he meet in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't leave my car. He would usually go to the municipal building. I don't know who he met with because I remained in the car. He would go into the municipal building to see people there, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When he went to Banja Luka, did you travel alone with him or was Dr. Stakic sometimes in the company of others having the same destination in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most often, he would go alone. Sometimes he was accompanied by one of his vice-presidents, either Travar in charge of finances or Savanovic. So there were a few people. Some would accompany him sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was he ever accompanied by Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know Mr. Drljaca very well at that time. I only met him later. Mr. Drljaca, he had his own car and he would usually go alone. I didn't see Dr. Stakic socialising with him. And if Stakic came, then Drljaca would also sometimes come on his own accompanied by his own people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see him together -- or was he accompanied in his car by one of the following persons: Mr. Arsic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that person. Only later I heard that he held a post in the army. That's what I heard when I went to the front line, but I never met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Kovacevic later on. He was sitting in a different office. I believe he was the president of the Executive Board. His office was next to Stakic's office, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been to the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very rarely, maybe once or twice. But there was no need for me to go up there. Us drivers would be sitting in the janitor's room waiting for our instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you waited for your instruction, for example, and, say, Dr. Stakic didn't arrive as envisaged, would you give him a direct call or the secretary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had his own secretary who would call him. I was sitting down there, and if he didn't arrive, then if I was given to drive somebody else, I would drive that person. There was no need for me to wait for Stakic if I had other things to do, then there would be other persons driving him when he showed up later. So there was none of us assigned to a particular person. We would drive people as the need arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was the car used a sign of the importance of the person you drove? Was there a kind of hierarchy among the cars that, for example, the most important person would drive the Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no special marks. I had an old Jetta. Later on, I swapped with my colleague. That was only a month later. I swapped a car with a Mile Bogunovic so that the president would be driven in a better car rather than in an old Jetta. That's why I swapped cars with this man some month or a month and a half later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Swapping cars, you would say, if I understood you correctly, that from that point on, you drove Dr. Stakic in a Mercedes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first drove him in a Jetta, and later on I swapped cars with Bogunovic because his car was better. The Jetta was some 15 years old. And that's why I traded cars with this Bogunovic who had a better car, a Mercedes. And after that time, I drove the Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So approximately - I know it's a long time ago and it's difficult to recall - but at what point in time would it be that you started driving Dr. Stakic with a Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the 20th of June, or thereabouts. 20th of June, a month and a half after I started working in the Jetta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me now continue with the question who maybe was accompanying Dr. Stakic on one of the journeys? Was there -- did you ever see a Dr. -- not doctor, sorry. Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never met Radovan [As interpreted]. Only four or five years Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. later did I actually find out who Radoslav Brdjanin was. But I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: General Momir Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him. I heard that he was in Banja Luka, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him once. I also don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall at what occasion this was that you met Mr. Karadzic? Was it together with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that I saw him in Prijedor once if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At what point in time, please, and was it together with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that it was in 1992 when he arrived in Prijedor. I don't remember the date, but I believe that there was Krajisnik, Karadzic, and Biljana together in the new hotel in Prijedor, but I can't remember the date. It seems to me that they stayed there for a day or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a special occasion, a meeting of party or ARK or whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have that information. I only know that they came to visit. I believe that that was that. I don't know. I'm not a member of any party. I don't understand politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw her together with Karadzic and the other man. What's his name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Krajisnik maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Krajisnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you mentioned beforehand when driving to Banja Luka, you visited the municipal building. Are you quite sure that this was the municipal building, or was it for the purpose of visiting higher-ranking persons such as those just mentioned before in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was the municipal building. I know that building very well. He would enter the building, and I would wait in front of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And whom would Dr. Stakic meet there in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the car. I didn't get off the car. I didn't go with him. My job was to sit in the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For how long did you work as Dr. Stakic's driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that day, when I started, that is, the 17th of May, until about the 20th of September or October. I can't remember exactly. And that was the end of it. I was called up by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you return as a driver to the municipality of Prijedor after the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I returned in 1995, in March, or perhaps February. I returned and was a driver again, and I started -- took over my old job. I became the driver and still drive the president of the municipality and I drive him now as I did all those years earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In 1995, the president was again Dr. Stakic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When I returned, he was not the president. It was Kurnoga who was the president then. Stakic was not the president when I came. Then I must have gone wrong somewhere. It was Kurnoga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall that -- I refer to transcript page 10.344 to 345 of the transcript, for the parties only. Do you recall that Stakic and the driver was arrested or taken to custody by some Serb paramilitary forces? Do you recall such an incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't. I wasn't there. Seems that I was mistaken when I said that he wasn't there when I came. I don't remember any of that. Then I must have come in 1996 -- or wait. 1992, 1993, 1995. 1995 or 1996? I can't remember. 1996. I returned in 1996. 1996, yes, that's right. I started working in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to those places Dr. Stakic visited in 1992 when it was not necessary, for example, because the factory or the organisation was that close that it was possible to go by foot, better even to go by foot. What were these other companies Dr. Stakic would visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, mostly as I said, he would go to the mines, Zitopromet, and then he couldn't walk there because the public amenities and Zitopromet, they are further away so that he would take the car. The school is nearby. The school is nearby. He could walk there. The court building is nearby, too. But there was nothing specific. He would just walk there because it was all around the corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You just said he would go -- let's start with this, "go to the mines." What do you have in mind and recall when you say he would go to the mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the mines as such, the building of the mines, the mine building. That is, the mine administration. Ostoja Marijanovic was the manager, and he was one of the first people that I met because I drove him around. Ostoja Marjanovic was the manager, if I remember well, and Balaban, I also remember him. He was another engineer. There were about five or six engineers who had worked in the mine and he went to see him but I didn't accompany him there. I would either be in the municipal hall or sit in the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, did you ever go to Ljubija together with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never went to Ljubija with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Kozarac with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never went to Kozarac, but we did go through Kozarac. We did go through Kozarac, but not to Kozarac. We never went to Kozarac. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At what period in time was it, to the best of your recollection, when you went to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've never been in Kozarac. We never stopped there. We would only go through Kozarac on our way to Banja Luka because the road goes through the place. But I was never in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On this route, did you ever see destroyed buildings, destroyed churches, destroyed mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. As we would travel through, and I know even the date more or less. That was the -- it seems that it was the 30th of April when the two of us were travelling from Omarska to Prijedor, there were barricades in Kevljani, which is right before Kozarac. And that is when we went from Omarska to Prijedor. There were barricades on the road, and 20 soldiers with weapons were there. And we passed through. In front of us was a Sarajevo car. And we passed through that morning at half past 8.00 on our way to Prijedor. And that day, the -- it seems that the attack took place on Prijedor that very morning. I remember that because I was in the municipal hall, and I was asleep when the attack happened because there was a bed for me in the municipal hall. If I had to stay late, then I would sleep there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it possible that you are confusing dates? Because you are mentioning the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May, the 30th of May, the 30th of May. That's when that was because in April I wasn't working at all, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently this special tour was in fact also for you something special. Could you please go into some more details of this tour you took that date around Kozarac on, as you stated, your way to Banja Luka. What happened? Was your car controlled? If yes, by whom? Were there any other problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stopped us down there in the village of Kevljani. It's right before Kozarac some 10 kilometres from Omarska. And the barricades with iron rods had already been put up there. And that morning, as we went through, the barricades were already on the road, and they stopped us there. And there was a car there, an Audi 100, with Sarajevo plates was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there. And I was behind it. They stopped that car, and we stopped behind the Audi. They didn't ask for the papers. They let through the one before us and then let us through. So that was that morning. And I remember that the next morning, we couldn't get through because the exchange of fire had started by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You stated "they didn't let us through," "they stopped." Who were "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms, had automatic weapons. They were those Muslims. I couldn't recognise them because they all had uniforms and green berets. They were Berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then it would be your testimony the next day you faced other problems. You said "We couldn't get through." What did you do in this situation when you couldn't get through? Did you take another route or what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around half past 1.00 that day, we could not get back from Prijedor to Omarska. So we took a round about route through Petrovo Selo, Maricka, and so on to get back to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When visiting mines, did you also visit the Omarska iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No. I never went to the Omarska mine, not even near it, because we went through Maricka, which is on the other side to get to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Keraterm building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I've never been to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When driving around the Prijedor town as such, did you ever notice buildings destroyed in the war operations and where was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That morning, at half past 4.00, I was asleep in the municipal hall. But it was the 1st of June. The attack happened at half past 4.00. One could hear a powerful detonation. Something serious had gone off. And I jumped off the bed dressed up. I didn't know what was happening. It was foggy, and there was rain. I remember there was drizzle. Black smoke. Something was firing. The glass panes shattered on the windows because that day, the municipal hall and the SUP were attacked. And the hotel, I couldn't really see what was on fire. I could see that something was burning towards the -- I could see this dense smoke coming towards the municipal hall. But later on I learned that the hotel had been set on fire, and the old hotel called Ribar, that was also on fire. But there was gun fire. There were quite a number of dead people in front of the municipal hall. I could see five or six policemen there dead. I was watching through the window. It was lasting for quite a time. Many people died in front of the municipal hall. They could not be helped because there was a sniper. It was only around 10.00 or past 9.00 that an ambulance car arrived. I could see through the fire and all that they were picking up both the living and the dead and they took them away. And only around 11.00 or 12.00 the situation calmed down slightly so that one could see what was happening and it was then that I saw the hotel was on fire. And it was like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see the destruction of Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see Stari Grad because I stayed where I was. I dared not come out. I stayed in the municipal hall because -- I didn't go to Stari Grad. I didn't go anywhere from the municipal hall. I was in the municipal hall all the time because there was gunfire. One could hear detonations, and I never went anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the aftermath of these special events, was Dr. Stakic at all interested in seeing what had happened and asking you, therefore, to drive him to these places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. Like me, because he didn't dare. There was gunfire all around. We were imprisoned, our 6 or 7, in the municipal hall, we simply couldn't get out. Until noon we didn't dare put our heads out because there were snipers firing all the time. There was chaos, and the police was in the chaos so we dared not go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic at any point in time show interest in what happened in the Omarska camp, in the Keraterm camp, in Trnopolje camp, asking you "Let's go there and see what's happening there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, I never went to any camp, Keraterm or that, what's it, Trnopolje or Omarska. I was only once sent to take something or drive a repairman to Trnopolje. That was when I went there once, and I saw those civilians walking around the school and the culture centre. I stayed there because the electricians were repairing something or not. I can't remember exactly why I took those people to Trnopolje, but later on, I saw people in Trnopolje. There were lots of them around the school, around the culture centre, around the playground. There were 500 or perhaps a thousand people, people were coming and going, passing through. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to the initial question, could it happen that also other drivers were asked to drive Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so because I suppose he would have asked me to come with him because I drove him around. I don't think that anyone else drove him but me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where did Dr. Stakic live precisely in -- you said you started the 17th of May, 1992. Yes, yes, that's right. That day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where did he live precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly when I was there, he was living in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where in Omarska, please? The concrete address.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are no streets there. He was renting a place at those two sisters. He was living with his family on the upper floor across the street from Mile Rosic's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Across the street from Mile Rosic's house or beside the house of Mile Rosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to Mile Rosic's house, right next to it. Just a low hedge between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the same side of the road. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same side. The same everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic at any point in time move to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this attack on Prijedor and the rest, Stakic had a flat somewhere around the hospital or the health centre. I don't know, but he had a flat somewhere there behind the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you then pick him up in the morning from the place behind the health centre and bring him back to this place in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was -- I don't really know where that flat is. He walked to his workplace in the morning, and I made it from Omarska in different ways because the car was in front of the municipal hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever drive with Dr. Stakic to Cirkin Polje, the building of the Crisis Staff in Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never took him to Cirkin Polje. I don't know if he went there with somebody else. He didn't with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever go together with Dr. Stakic to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've never been to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very practical question: When you had to refuel your car, how did this take place? Where did you have to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had coupons for fuel in Brezicani, and we could get the fuel at all the petrol pumps in Prijedor. We would be issued with coupons and get our fuel at a petrol station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who issued these coupons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official person, the cashier. He would issue it for 200 or 500 marks' worth, and you go there, you get your fuel, you come back, and you settle all the accounts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who are these official persons you mentioned just before? Where would you get these coupons or vouchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would get them in the office upstairs, from the cashier's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. office. There were two cashiers in the financial department. There were two of them. And they issued you. They either give you money in advance, some down payment or coupons. You go there. You're given that. You sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be quite concrete, was it in the office of Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic? I make reference to the witness testimony transcript page 7537.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic, I've never heard of him working in the municipal hall. What I heard about him was that he was in Trnopolje. That's when I heard about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What did he do in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. All I heard is that he was sort of a manager of that camp. It wasn't a camp, a reception centre or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to the vouchers, what was printed on the vouchers? Who was issuing the vouchers? Was it the municipality, was it the Crisis Staff, or what was it? What could you read on these vouchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could read "petrol," "petrol Brezicani" and these were the vouchers which you could use to get the fuel and be issued with an invoice. They could only be used for fuel. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you go to -- with these vouchers to any of the petrol stations in Prijedor or the surroundings, or was this limited to certain petrol stations in Prijedor or in the municipality? Or were they valid all over Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in Prijedor on the Banja Luka Road at their petrol station. You couldn't use them anywhere else. There are two petrol stations at the railway station, and this one here. And whichever had the fuel, that is where we went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be the one -- we are aware that there's at least one petrol station on Banja Luka Road, and your testimony is that it would be the one close to the railway station. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There is a petrol station in Prijedor across the street from the railway station, and there is this one on the Banja Luka Road. And in Kozarac, also, there was a station that belonged to them. But it wasn't operational because it had been put on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see wearing Dr. Stakic a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stakic as a rule wore a suit. He usually wore a suit. At times I saw him in a uniform, but there would be some troops, some recruits. When they would be going, he would put the uniform then on, on such special occasions, or when he went to lay a wreath down. He would wear a uniform only on some official ceremonial occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true, as we heard it from several witnesses, that there was a special period in time that staff members and officials were asked and required to wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't such a request. Because, for instance, I was the driver. I never had a uniform because it would not say so anywhere. Nobody had taken a decision. We mostly wore civilian clothes as we drove those cars. There were no ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When wearing a uniform, did Dr. Stakic at the same time wear a pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he carried a pistol on those occasions when he wore a uniform. He had a pistol. So he had a pistol when he had a uniform. But that happened seldom. It was very seldom that he put on the uniform. And so he also had a pistol, a reserve one, because there were all sorts of gangs around. One had to have a pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell me why it was that Dr. Stakic would have to go to, as you said, some troops, some recruits, when he went to lay a wreath down? What was it that brought Dr. Stakic to visit the military forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what he had to do. It was up to me to take him there when a wreath would be laid. Whether he was asked to wear a uniform, I don't know. I only know that he wore a uniform very seldom. He mostly wore very nice civilian clothes, a suit. He only wore a uniform twice or three times as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But leaving aside the question of uniform for just a moment, what was it, why was it necessary to visit military forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never drove any military forces. I don't know where they were. I went to the army myself. When I drove him, we never visited the troops or the military force. I was in the army myself later on, but I myself never took him or anywhere to visit the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Stanar, during your testimony this morning, I had the impression that related to certain periods of time, you were a little bit confused, and therefore, I have to restart the line of questions once more. Could you please tell us when leaving the area where you were no longer welcome and coming then to the municipality of Prijedor, at which point in time was it that you arrived in Omarska? And where did you live in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Omarska from the year 1960 up to this very day at the address Prvomajska 147 in the centre of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This morning, you mentioned that beforehand, you were gainfully employed elsewhere. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this was -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished school in Omarska, that is, elementary school. As far as I remember, it was in 1968. It was a long time ago. I was in Prijedor in 1969, 1970, and 1971. And 1971, I started working in the mine for a year. In 1973, I joined the army. In 1975, after the army, I left for Slovenia where I stayed up until the year 1990. After the year 1990, when I was fired in Ljubljana, which was due to the beginning of unrest in the former Yugoslavia, Ljubljana decided to get rid of us, especially of us from Bosnia. I was without work, so I returned to Prijedor. In Prijedor, when I started working in 1990 and 1991, I worked as a haulier with my old truck. Then when there was an opening in the municipality, I applied for that job. I was sent by the employment bureau to start working there as a driver. I've always been a professional driver. I was in Iraq for one or two times. I am a professional driver, and that's why I was employed in the municipality. I have worked as a driver for over 30 years now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please try to recall once again the period of time of importance for us is not the time when you got the aforementioned decision, but when did you actually start being a driver in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17 May, 1992. I was issued a decision to start working as a driver in the municipality of Prijedor. I have that paper at home. I forgot to take it with me. I should have, but I can fax it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One thing is a decision; another issue, when did you actually start working? Was there maybe a period of test before you started based on this decision as of the 17th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of May 17, for a month, I was on a trial period. That was that. And that's the only thing I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let us please know where did you live in Omarska when you came back from Ljubljana? How far was it away from the house where Dr. Stakic and his family lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 400 or 500 metres. I had my own house. I built my own house in Omarska in 1982. My father also has his own house where I had lived together with my father. He built that house in 1960, and I built my house in 1982, and that's when I moved into my own house from my father's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you during the period of time when first coming back from Ljubljana, and then arriving in Prijedor, did you visit sometimes your relatives Dr. Stakic and maybe a little bit further away in the relationship, Milan Rosic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Stakic from his university days, from his student days. He would sometimes as a student come to visit my father. He was living in Banja Luka, graduated from med school, and then he started working -- I know that he worked in Omarska, in Prijedor, and in Teslic. He worked as a doctor. Whenever he came to Omarska, whenever I came from Slovenia, we socialised. We played football, we shot pools, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This morning, your testimony, page 6, line 6, you mentioned: "Since I lived in Omarska and he lived in Omarska, he would call me so if he could go back home." Let us try to fix these dates where you would drive Dr. Stakic from Omarska or back to Omarska a little bit more precisely. Was it days, weeks, or months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 17 May up to the 1st or the 2nd June, I would regularly take him from Omarska to Prijedor and back. After that, after the attack on Prijedor, we no longer drove there because he lived in Prijedor. He had an apartment there, whereas I travelled from Omarska to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be the route you took from Omarska to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would take the old road and a couple of days later, the only -- it was passable. But it wasn't safe. So I did what I could. I would sometimes take my own car, sometimes I would drive with my colleague. The situation was bad. Due to the situation, it was difficult and dangerous to travel. There were all sorts of people along the road. There were armed people, thieves, gangs. There were all sorts of people, and I was really scared when I had to travel to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that you travelled the route through Lamovita, Kamicani, Kozarac, Kozarusa, Orlovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are exactly the places that I passed. And in Orlovci, there was a checkpoint, a police checkpoint. There were always six or seven people there. This is where the police manned a checkpoint, and they checked everybody who entered or was leaving Prijedor. You couldn't just go through. You had to wait because there was a checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was a checkpoint manned by regular police forces. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the regular police was manning that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then following your testimony that as from the 17th of May until approximately the 2nd of June, you would take together with Dr. Stakic the same aforementioned route. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was it who brought Dr. Stakic beforehand, before the 17th of May from Omarska to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I heard, I didn't work at that time. But I learned that it was Dragan Grandic who drove him. He was also a driver in the municipality. And he would also drive with Mile Rosic, the man who lived next to him. He worked in Prijedor, and the two of them would travel in Mile Rosic's car every day. When I started working, he stopped travelling with these two, and I started driving him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, before testifying today here, did you have any contacts with one of the parties, be it the Prosecution or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody paid me a visit. I was never with any of the parties. I'm here for the first time. Nobody ever visited me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss your testimony beforehand with other third persons such as Mr. Murselovic or Mr. Milan Rosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic found out that I would be travelling to The Hague; and since he had been here before, he told me, you shouldn't have a problem. You just go there and say whatever you know. I know that Mile Rosic also testified here. I saw him once or twice after that. And that's about all the people that I have seen. I haven't seen anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss during these meetings your testimony and/or the previous testimonies of, be it Mr. Murselovic or Milan Rosic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me anything. I didn't ask them anything either. I did not feel any need to ask them what had happened to them. It is up to me to say what I know. That's why I did not find it necessary to ask them anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it that on page 9 of today's testimony, line 21, 22, you started testifying about the 30th of April and the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 30th of April, as far as I remember, was when Prijedor was attacked. Or was it on the 1st of May or -- between the 30th of April and the 1st of May, I believe this was the attack on Prijedor. Maybe I'm mistaken, but that's as far as I can remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you were in Omarska already at that time waiting to be gainfully employed, were you aware about the so-called takeover of Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not informed about that. I was not interested in that. My only concern was work and what I would be living on. And I was not into politics at all. Only subsequently did I learn there had been a takeover of power in Prijedor, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know the role your relative Dr. Stakic played in Prijedor Municipality before April 30th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that he was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly while the president was -- let me think. Cehajic. Cehajic was president, and Stakic was vice-president. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who was president of the Assembly, the then-Serbian Assembly after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I don't know even to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was president of the Municipal Assembly when you started your work as you told us on the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milomir Stakic was appointed president as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you drive ever with Dr. Stakic to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Smederevo on two occasions. We were in Smederevo twice. Two cars went to Smederevo. One was driven by Milorad Sipka, and that car was a Golf, and us, representatives of the municipality, went with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these two visits to Smederevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't tell me anything. They didn't tell me why they went there. There was Marjanovic, Sipka, Balaban, people from the mines. So I suppose that their job was to discuss something to do with the mine, with the iron ore. But they didn't tell me anything, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to come back to a very special occasion. There is conflicting testimony, some discrepancies, from previous testimonies. The concrete question is did you ever drive Dr. Stakic to the Omarska camp? And maybe it can assist you, together with a high-ranking delegation from Banja Luka and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. While I drove, while I drove Dr. Stakic, he never went to Omarska. You call it a camp. I don't know. We would go home to Omarska, but he was never in the camp in Omarska. While I drove him, we were never there in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You were not only the driver, but also a relative to Dr. Stakic. Did you ever discuss the purpose of the camp and the atrocities indisputably happened in these camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he never talked to me about this camp. This was never a subject of our conversations while we were driving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If a witness would testify - I make reference to transcript pages 11.943 until 11.953, for example, if a witness would testify that Dr. Stakic following the takeover, this would be as of the 30th of April, did no longer regularly come back to Omarska, what would be your answer, if confronted with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that after the attack on Prijedor, Mr. Stakic did not go back to Omarska. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But the problem we have based on your testimony until now is, no doubt, whether it was the 30th of April, 1st of May, or the end of May you're referring to. Just recently you mentioned the 2nd of June. Is it possible that you confuse the two months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have not confused the dates. You suggested to me the 2nd of June. It was you who suggested it was the 2nd of June. But this was a mistake. In those months, I was -- I don't remember it well, but I know that after the 30th that I've mentioned, then you mentioned the 2nd of June which I accepted. But it wasn't the 2nd of June. No, it was not the 2nd of June I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So what was the concrete date you drove the last time Dr. Stakic from Omarska and back to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the 2nd of May. When the attack on Prijedor happened, after that, a few days after that, we did not take that route to Prijedor any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever drive, to change the issue, other members of the family of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never drove any member of the Stakic family except him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the entire family of Dr. Stakic, being a relative to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, we paid each other visits. I would come to his place and he'd come to mine. We visited one another now and then. But that was before all this happened. Ever since his student days, when he got married, and the war started in Teslic, then he came to Omarska. He and his wife would come to my place, to our place, to see my wife and me. And we were on good terms and so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For the moment, I have no further questions but I have to come back to this at a later period of time. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Stanar, you said that you were fired from your job at Ljubija mine because of your Serbian ethnicity. Who was the director of the mine at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a mistake, Your Honour. I didn't work in Ljubija. I did start working in Ljubija, but where I was fired was Ljubljana, not Ljubija. But before I went to do my military service, I worked in Ljubija, but that was a different thing. It wasn't the mine. I worked there with the fire place, and that is where I worked for about a year or 13 months and 11 days. And after that, in 1973, I went to do my regular military service. And after that, in 1975, I went to Ljubljana. And I worked there until 1990. And that is when I was fired, in Ljubljana, because of all those unrests. I then was allowed to return to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And when you returned to Bosnia, when did you start to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a truck. I was a haulier as of 1990, as of May. From 1990 to 1991, I worked as a haulier. And after that, his story, that is, this job at the municipal hall turned up, and I accepted to be a driver for the municipal hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And you worked as a driver in the Prijedor Municipality until what time, what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 20th of October, 1992. After that, I reported to a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Sorry, you reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received a summons from the military authorities, from those chief ones, and they requested that I join the army. The Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And in your testimony, you state that you worked as a driver of the municipality until June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the second -- no, I didn't say that. That must be a mistake. That was Omarska/Prijedor as I drove. But I worked until 1992, that is, until October as a driver. After 1992, I stopped working. I joined the army. That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And then after the army, you again --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the army, 1996, no, I've -- remembered, it wasn't 1995. [As interpreted] 1996 it was. After February, that's when I returned again to be the driver for the municipality, and that's what I do to this day, and I still drive around the president, Murselovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: At that time in 1996, who was the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Kurnoga. And after Kurnoga, Stakic became the president once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So you again became the driver for Dr. Stakic, yeah?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't his driver any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But you told that the president of the municipality was Kurnoga, and then after Kurnoga, Dr. Stakic again was elected as president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I don't remember that. I know that I no longer drive him -- I started driving when he was not the president any more as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me just continue for one other question. You mentioned that previous to the takeover, sometimes Dr. Stakic was taken by Mr. Rosic to Prijedor. This Mr. Milan Rosic testified the 6th of February, 2003, this is page 11.946 of the transcript, when asked by the Defence: "Can you tell us, sir, did at any time after April 30th, 1992, did you have an opportunity to drive Dr. Stakic to the city/town of Prijedor"? The answer was: "No, after that I didn't. A few days later, I didn't really see him." End of quote, just for the purpose. It was the next-door neighbour, he didn't see him any longer. Starting the quote again: "And then later on, I heard that he had an official driver who drove him around, and that he had an official car." Question: "Do you know, sir, the name of that driver that was officially driving Dr. Stakic around?" Answer: "Yes, Petar Stanar who still works in the municipality as a driver." So how is it possible that the next-door neighbour can't see any longer Dr. Stakic in Omarska and that your testimony today is that at that period of time, you drove on a daily basis Dr. Stakic from Omarska to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He drove him probably until the date when I started driving him. I know that Dragan Grandic, he's a driver who also drove him several times. But after the 17th, I started driving him, and I went on doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Even though it appears - we have to find the truth - if it appears that at that time, Dr. Stakic did no longer commute on a daily basis from Omarska to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't travel as of the 2nd or the 3rd. He stopped travelling. Until that day, I drove him regularly to Omarska and back. After that, he lived in Prijedor. We worked normally. I would come, I would drive, and went on driving him, until October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He didn't travel as of the 2nd or 3rd of which month, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the 2nd of March, but the 2nd of June, after the attack on Prijedor. For two or three days I didn't see him after that. After that, he moved house to Prijedor. He had a flat somewhere behind the health centre there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to come back to this later. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I only have a small question. Today we heard you -- you told us on page 35, line 14, that you were having conversations with Dr. Stakic while we were driving. That's your quote. What about? Can you tell me what -- which were the subjects of these conversations while you were driving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the subject, I'm not into politics, I know nothing about politics. I didn't want to know about it. It was mostly what we had done Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for the previous weekend, played football, had a walk, talked. Secondly, we never discussed politics. I don't go into it because I know nothing about it. And I didn't want to burden him with that, to ask him something unnecessary. I didn't think I should ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Were you asked to drive the car taking some important visitors around Prijedor, Prijedor town or Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't ever. I usually did the same thing. When he was in the office, I drove everybody else, the vice-president, the secretary, Travar, repairmen, whoever I was ordered to drive. I went wherever I was told to go. At times, two or three days would pass by without me driving him because I drove others, and that is how we always did it. We were five drivers there, and we all did everything. And if he went somewhere, then I would be issued with a travel order and take him there. But otherwise, I worked as all the other drivers. We had no privileges or anything. We all did the same kind of jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I probably wasn't very clear, but let me put an example. If there was a celebration in Prijedor town or an official ceremony, and some visitors were coming from other municipalities, say, Banja Luka or Sanski Most or whatever, were you asked, asked to drive these persons around to the ceremony or taking them back to the municipality or whatever could have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It wasn't mine to do it. Everybody who came to Prijedor had his own driver, and everybody went there in their own cars. So whenever they came to Prijedor, they would meet in the president's office when they would come to Prijedor, but nobody drove anybody anywhere because they all had their own drivers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that we are in the phase of rebuttal, the first line of question would be for the Prosecution now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the dates have been differing as you have been giving your testimony this morning. I want to try and place events in relation to things that happened in the municipality. But first, you said that you returned to the municipality around May 1990. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't return to the municipality in 1990. In 1990, I returned from Ljubljana. I said I returned to Prijedor, that is, home, in Omarska. And in 1990, I became a haulier. I had a truck, and I had the authorisation for 1991 to work as the haulier. It has not been written down accurately. I told you everything as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please listen to my question. If you don't understand my question, can you ask me to clarify it. My question was did you return to the Prijedor Municipality from Ljubljana around May 1990? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes, thereabouts. Not quite, yes, thereabouts. April, May, thereabouts. I didn't look up the dates, but there is a -- I've got a contract which shows when I started working as a haulier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that after that time, you heard that Cehajic became president. This is Professor Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about him because I had nothing to do with the municipality. I was a haulier. And it was -- I'd never tried for find anything about him. I was a haulier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please pause there. I want you to answer the questions that I ask you. And the question was, was it Professor Muhamed Cehajic that you heard took over -- became president of the Prijedor Municipality? It's a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that he had become the president. I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your testimony earlier that you heard that Cehajic was president. My question was, was it Professor Muhamed Cehajic, and this was at the time that Dr. Stakic became the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a different question. When that Cehajic was president, it was in 1992, isn't it? But while I worked, I didn't know Cehajic or the other one. That's a mistake. A driver, a haulier, has nothing to do with the municipality. It's another matter to be --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause, pause. I'm simply asking you whether the person - I'm not asking whether you know him personally. I'm asking you whether the person that you heard was president, you mentioned a person Cehajic. I'm asking you simply, was it Professor Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether he's professor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on. You said that on the 17th of May, 1992, you began working as a driver in the Municipal Assembly, and you did that until the 20th of October, 1992. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate. It's accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this morning that on the 30th of May, when you were driving Dr. Stakic from Omarska to Prijedor at around 8.30 a.m. in the morning, you were stopped at barricades near Kevljani. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No date, that was the attack -- yes, it is correct. Yes, yeah. It is. 8.30, Kevljani, we started for Prijedor at 8.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You said the date was the 30th of May, but I'm wondering whether you are confused about the date. Do you recall the attack on Kozarac on the 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. I forgot that. Yes, I realise -- see, I forgot it. The 24th, yes, seven days before the attack on Prijedor. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were stopped at the barricades at 8.30 in the morning, was this before the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack on Kozarac happened later, from what I heard. About 1.00 or half past 1.00, and we passed through at half past 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that you drove Dr. Stakic to work from Omarska, from the 17th of May until the attack on Prijedor when he moved into an apartment behind the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes that's right. That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to this apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never drove there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that around the 20th of June, 1992, you swapped cars with Mile Bogunovic, and you started driving the Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true. I swapped cars because he had a better car. My car was old. We swapped. He gave me his car, and I gave him mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So up until that time, whenever you drove Dr. Stakic, you were driving the Jetta, and from the 20th of June onwards, you always drove him in the Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I drove him in a Mercedes from then on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you drove other people around, the vice-president, Mr. Travar. When you would drive them around, would you drive them in the Jetta and leave the Mercedes in case Dr. Stakic needed to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, unless there was -- unless agreed otherwise, I drove everybody in the Mercedes ever since I got that Mercedes. I didn't change cars ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you received fuel coupons. Did you see who signed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see who signed them. But the coupon is a coupon is a coupon. It has a stamp and seal, and it says what the value is, and petrol, nothing else. And there were those of 50, 100, 20, and 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever fill your car up at the petrol station in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never went to get fuel in Tukovi. I did in Brezicani, down there where they have the depot, because at times, there was no fuel. So we got the fuel directly from there when the stations were out of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that you drove Dr. Stakic to lots of different institutions. Did you ever drive him to the Kozarski Vjesnik, Radio Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prijedor offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radio Prijedor, he went there, yes. Kozarski Vjesnik, no. Radio -- he went to the radio station when they invited him several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you drive him to the Radio Prijedor offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once a week, twice a week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every fortnight I'd say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever drive him to the SDS offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where that office is. I don't even know. I never asked, and I don't know where that office is. Because I know nothing about those parties, and I don't know what party he was a member of. It seems that he was a radical in my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive him to the building across from the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never drove him to Keraterm, to that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
