utterances.text: No, please listen to my question. Did you drive him to a building which was opposite the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never drove him to that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that Stakic wore a uniform when he went to see the troops or the new recruits. Did you drive him to the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't drive him up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he see the troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The troops, he didn't visit the troops anywhere. It was all the army, and I mixed them up because the troops, the young ones drive around there. But it wasn't like that then. It was the troops -- everybody was the troops then. And those were the events, the day of the combatants day, laying wreaths on a monument and one dresses up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you mean this morning when you said he would wear a uniform when he went to see troops or new recruits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand. I mean, the uniform, well, one put it on an important date, when somebody -- I said, when wreaths are laid, when somebody is invited to something. That's when one puts the uniform on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. The Trial Chamber, after deliberation, decided that it would be necessary now to give a warning to the witness. Rule 91 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides that the Chamber proprio motu may warn a witness of the duty to tell the truth and the consequences that may result from a failure to do so. The maximum penalty for false testimony under solemn declaration shall be a fine of 100.000 Euros or a term of imprisonment of seven years or both. A number of discrepancies in your own testimony, and in conjunction with other testimonies, leads us to this warning. And we really have to ask you to tell us the truth and nothing but the truth. So please beware that if you so want, we may confront you with the one or other video telling us something else that is in contradiction with your testimony. But please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, because this is not the Defence witness, I was reluctant at that time to intervene, and I would like my learned colleague to say the page number and the line number when she puts in front of the witness what he said. And from the page 27, line 9, in the transcript, it says some troops, some recruits, but at that time, the witness said only "the recruits," meaning new soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't recall this, and we have the transcript before us, and you quoted quite correctly from the transcript. Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what events would Dr. Stakic wear a uniform to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've just told you, he would put a uniform on on very few occasions. I only saw him in a uniform very rarely. When there was certain events, he would wear that uniform, and I didn't lie when I say that. This is the truth. He wore the uniform very rarely, only for official things. That's when I would see him wearing the uniform, and that is that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, again, please listen to my question. My question was what events would Dr. Stakic wear a uniform to? What are the official occasions that he wore a uniform to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would wear a uniform to receive a military delegation or when he would lay flowers on the monument or when he would go to the barracks. That's when he would wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did he go to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very seldom. I saw him only a few times when he went to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this, the time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the dates. In any case, I would drive him there, and I would wait in the car for him to come back after having had his conversation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever drive him to Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Dr. Stakic wore a pistol when he wore a uniform. Did you see him carry a pistol when he was wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When he wore civilian clothes, I didn't see him carrying a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you your pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got it from the municipality. Actually, they sent me to the SUP to get the official pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the 30th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of a weapon was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a 7.62 pistol, a military-type, a TT762. That's what it says on it, an old model.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say after the 30th, do you mean after the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was after the attack on Prijedor that I received this pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Argibay asked you a question about the conversations that you had with Dr. Stakic when you were driving around. And you said that they were mostly about playing football or what happened on the weekend, and they didn't have anything to do with politics. During the five months that you drove Dr. Stakic around, did you ever ask him if he knew what happened to Muhamed Cehajic, the person whose job he had taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him about that. I didn't know the man. I don't know. I didn't ask him anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you didn't ask him, did Dr. Stakic ever mention it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention any of his -- he didn't talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever drive Dr. Stakic to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the other four drivers drove Dr. Stakic to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and as far as I've heard, nobody ever took him to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 13 this morning, you said that you drove Dr. Stakic to the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly building where he was -- I think you said where he was needed. How often did you go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not often, a couple of times I went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was in May or June or July? Was it shortly after you started work as a driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact dates. But it was on a couple of occasions that I took him to Banja Luka. When, I don't know. Whether it was soon after or later on, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Mico Kovacevic, the president of the Executive Board, did he ever accompany you to Banja Luka with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't go to Banja Luka with us. That is, when I drove him. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you drove from Prijedor to Banja Luka, you would have driven past the Keraterm. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned later on subsequently where Keraterm was. Yes, it is on that road some hundred or two hundred metres away from that road. And obviously, yes, we did pass by that when we went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that you saw destruction of houses in Kozarac on your way to Banja Luka. Did you see the same destruction in the villages next to Kozarac, that is, Kamicani and Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't, because as we were passing through Kozarac and Kamicani on the way to Banja Luka, one could see that there were houses destroyed and burned down if they were close to the road. And that is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive Dr. Stakic to Pale on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a delegation from Banja Luka attending the Prijedor Municipal Assembly building in mid-July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only if that was the delegation that I've already mentioned, that stayed in the Prijedor hotel in 1992. That was Karadzic, Biljana, and that third man. That is the only delegation that I know visited Prijedor. Maybe that was that delegation. And I've mentioned that delegation. I'm not sure of the date. It was in 1992. The third man was Momir Krajisnik [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that towards the end of your -- of you working as a driver or earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thereabouts, afterwards. I can't remember very well, but I know that I was there, and that is sure. But I don't know the date. It was in 1992, and I'm sure of that. It was certainly in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't recall any other delegation coming from Banja Luka around the middle of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know him either. I heard of all these people later on. I didn't know them at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from any of the other four drivers about a delegation coming from Banja Luka and visiting the Omarska camp in mid-July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear that from any of the drivers. And I personally cannot remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the janitor's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the same place on the left-hand side as you enter the town hall, the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was on the ground level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if a lot of luxury vehicles pulled up outside the front of the municipal assembly, would you recall something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. There were always vehicles, a lot of vehicles were always parked there. So it's very hard to recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were luxury vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the vehicles are luxury vehicles, and there are a lot of them parked in front of the municipal building at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When people who were driven to the municipal building, when they came to the building, where did their drivers go? Did they wait in the janitor's room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would mostly remain sitting in their cars, or they would come to the basement. There's a cafe there. They would have a cup of coffee. In the janitor's room, there's just the janitor -- actually, two of them, two janitors. And drivers would either sit in their cars or go downstairs to the basement to have a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified earlier this morning, and I don't recall the page, that the drivers got their instructions from your superior, Zeljko Grahovac, in the janitor's room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 14, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified earlier this morning that you received your instructions in the janitors' room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Grahovac had his own office on the first floor. I would be sitting in the janitors' office. When he needed to give me instructions, he would call me upstairs to his office. So he would not come to the janitors' office to give me instructions. It was the other way around. I would go upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you and yourself and the other four drivers would spend your time, when you weren't sent on an assignment, in the janitors' office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the basement drinking coffee, in the janitors' office, or in the front of the building sitting in the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. When you were downstairs in the basement having coffee, did you see drivers from any other municipalities, for example, Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Krupa, Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know these drivers. I was a new, a new driver. And I did not know these drivers well. I only knew those four who worked with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even if you didn't know them personally, did you see drivers from other municipalities who had brought people to the Prijedor Municipality building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw drivers, but I didn't know them personally. I didn't know any other drivers but the ones whom I got to know when I joined them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Drago Mandic and a person named Mile Bogunovic. And you mentioned a person named Miro. Do you recall now his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Miro Bjelanovic and this is not Dragan Mandic, but Dragan Grandic, Grandic. And Miro Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a person named Ergelic. Do you also recall his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember, but he left for America. He stayed on after me, and then left for America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing foreign journalists visit the Municipal Assembly building in -- around the beginning of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from any of the other four drivers about these international journalists visiting Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive Dr. Stakic to Maricka village for the second anniversary of the SDS around the end of July, beginning of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take him to Maricka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever drive Dr. Stakic to the Manjaca camp in the Banja Luka Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were never in Manjaca in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around the 20th to the 25th of August, did you ever drive Dr. Stakic to the military barracks in Banja Luka or in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never in Doboj or in the military barracks in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would Dr. Stakic leave the Municipal Assembly building in the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely. He would seldom go places. He would spend more time in the municipality, and people would come to see him. Only when we had to go to Banja Luka or to Smederevo, then I would receive an order, and I would take him. And that's where he would go out for a day or two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever pick up Dr. Stakic from the SUP building? I'm sorry, it's across the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's across the road. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever pick him up from the fish restaurant near the hospital, the restaurant called Oskar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did go there on several occasions when he would have lunch there, I would go to Oskar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people that he would be having lunch with on the occasions you went to pick him up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mostly stayed in the car. I didn't get out of the car. And I didn't see the people who he was sitting with. And mind you, I hadn't been there for 20 years, and I didn't know people very well. I knew a few people who worked with him in the municipality, and I know that he had lunch with them in Oskar. Sometimes people from Zitopromet, he would go to see the director of that company, Mr. Vasa Cvijic, and he would sometimes have lunch with him as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever take or pick up Dr. Stakic from the Tri Asa restaurant in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions, he went there to have lunch. When we were returning from Banja Luka on several occasions, we would have lunch there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else did you see Dr. Stakic having lunch with in the Tri Asa restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people he travelled with, and there was also the boss of that restaurant, Nijaz Gazic [phoen], and very few other people. Maybe sometimes Nedjo Delic. He is the owner of Evropa. We would sometimes go to his place, sometimes for lunch or dinner. These were the two restaurants which were open, and where you could have either breakfast or lunch. There very few restaurants open in Prijedor, maybe two or three more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier this morning at page 31 that you used to shoot pool with Dr. Stakic. Who were the other persons that you both played with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly my colleagues from Omarska, my neighbour Novo Skake married the son of the boss. Mostly the colleagues that we knew. There was a pool table in Tri Asa, and on Saturdays and Sundays when we didn't work, we would shoot some pools there. And there were very few places where you could go out to and spend time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Simo Drljaca play pool with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca was not with us at that time. I didn't know him at that time. It was only later on that I found out who Simo Drljaca was. I met him later on, and then they told me, well, this is Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, besides the 7.62 millimetre pistol, were you given any other weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't given any other weapon. That was the only one I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you went to Smederevo on two occasions with Mr. Marjanovic. Is that in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, yes. Via Belgrade, you go through Belgrade, and then Smederevo comes after it. It's in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go in Smederevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hotel was -- the steel works in Smederevo. I don't know where that is. I think it's Smederevo, some rail carriages, steel works, something like that. I didn't go in. I was in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the Municipal Assembly. Can you tell the Court what you did on a normal day. You arrived at work at 7.00 a.m. What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you have your coffee. If there is nothing to do, then you wait either in the cafeteria downstairs or at the janitor's, drop by. If there is something to do, perhaps I'm given the instruction to drive that person, so I go, I come back. And then 10 or 15 times a day, take the cleaning woman there, or take the janitor, because there's always some problem here, some problem there. Always lots of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taking them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if something's wrong, to have it repaired, or I take the mechanic to repair it. Or if need be, if necessary, I take somebody to the bank. Or if one has to go and get coupons, then I go and get that. So whatever there was to do, I had to be there, and I had to go wherever they sent me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you drive the most in the Municipal Assembly building? What person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't keep a record. I drove people. I was at the disposal of everybody who worked in the municipality -- in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you act as a courier and deliver messages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the messenger was a messenger, and he's got his job. I only drove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the messenger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember who was the messenger then. I know who it is now, but I can't remember who it was then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have to deliver documents to anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing important, no, I didn't have to do it. Always something trivial, I didn't have anything important to take to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that you were busy for most of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at times, there was more work; at times, there was less work. At times, there wasn't really much to do. So sometimes there was a lot of work, and sometimes there wasn't. So you sit and wait.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the same for the other four drivers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same, same. We all did the same kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's first turn to the unanswered questions. Further questions by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On page 48, you were asked, line 12, "What are the official occasions that Dr. Stakic wore a uniform to?" Answer: "He would wear a uniform to receive military delegations." What kind of military delegation, composed of whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mean that. Now, it turns out that that was that way. But it was the welcoming party. When one says military delegation, it's when the army is celebrating something or when there is a review. That's what I meant. Nobody else. When the army has its day, its celebration, that's what the delegation -- that's what one calls a delegation. I don't understand anything else. So that is that delegation. They get together, and they take flowers there and that's it. I didn't mean anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But these were your own words "military delegation." On what level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's how I said, military delegation. Since I was with the army later on, when somebody more important comes, so when one of the superiors comes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who were those superiors and superior to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whom do you mean? What superior officers? Stakic went, for instance, to visit them. If he went to the barracks, he would go there. And if there was a review, then that was that. That's what is called a delegation. These are the seniors that I meant, commander, his deputy, if that is what you had in mind, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not what I have in mind. But I want to ask you whom did you see there? Whom did Dr. Stakic meet there that you call military delegation, superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'd take him there, and I'd stand -- a military delegation is how shall I put it, the commander of the barracks. That's the military delegation, the barracks commander. Right, so that is where the review Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was and where people was lined up, and there was nothing else but that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was the barracks commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps it was Rajlic. I don't know. I didn't know those people. It seems to me -- I think it was Rajlic. Rajlic, Rajlic. Or Zeljaja, or Radmilo Zeljaja. He was, too. That's what I learned. I didn't really know that much. I didn't really know that many people. That's what I heard, Radmilo Zeljaja and Rajlic, the two of them, they were the number ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion when Dr. Stakic went to meet, call it, armed forces together with Mr. Arsic, addressing these military personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what they talked about. I'd take him there, and I'd wait until he finishes his conversation, and then I take him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then let's turn to another delegation you were, in fact, aware of. You spoke about Karadzic - it's on LiveNote today, page 51, line 14 - you said: "That was Karadzic, Biljana -" I think was Biljana you speak about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And that third man, and later you said Momir Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krajisnik, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And once again, the attempt, you left your job because you were mobilised exactly when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mobilisation, when I left, that was -- that was sometime -- the mobilisation was sometime in December. I reported to the unit -- I mean, I reported to the unit in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And approximately what was the last day you drove Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: October, September, November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October. I think it was in October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then this meeting in 1992 where there was a delegation in Prijedor Hotel composed of Karadzic, Plavsic, and Krajisnik, was it in October, September, or even earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. But I know that it happened. I can't give you the date because I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At that point in time, you were still the driver of Dr. Stakic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said you started the 17th of May driving Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of a Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the beginning, I didn't know what it was. But later on, I found out what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a group of people who bring authority, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be correct that the Crisis Staff was established by an order of 20 May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I know nothing about that. I know it existed, but I don't know when it was founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You testified that during this period of time, you brought Dr. Stakic from Omarska to Prijedor and back. Did it happen that the one or other day, Dr. Stakic had to leave later than usual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At times, he stayed longer. He wouldn't go back at 3.00, that he'd be kept at a meeting longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic ever on a night shift in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about his being on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know that Dr. Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. Afterwards, I heard some details, but was it he or somebody else, it seems to me, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But wouldn't it be correct that you, as a driver, should know and especially that you should know when it was to bring Dr. Stakic as it is still your testimony to Omarska during then maybe even nighttime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Never at night. It was almost as a rule, the working hours, perhaps a couple of hours longer, but we didn't travel by night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the municipal building, was there something like a communications centre for the Crisis Staff? Maybe to refresh your recollection, in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there's still something down there. I don't know what. But there's still something down there, something like a communications centre or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic going to this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see him going to that place, but he also came to have coffee like we did because I often slept there. There was my bed there, and I slept there on a number of occasions, if that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be your testimony that this place where you slept on several occasions, it was within this special communications centre or close to this centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was down there, in the basement, in the cellar. Everything was down there, the room where you could lie down, under the ground in the cellar. You had two beds there, so you could lie down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What could be the reason that you had to sleep there when it was for you to drive Dr. Stakic home day by day after the office hours, as you testified previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to spend the night there on a couple of occasions when it was dangerous, when the attack happened, that is when I spent some -- one or two nights there because I dared not go home. It was dangerous to go home at that time, and that is why I spent those nights there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't understand this answer. You lived in Omarska. You told us that you drove Dr. Stakic to Omarska. Why was it then that you had to spend nights in the municipal building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't go home. When I had nothing to get home with, that is when I stayed to spend the night in Prijedor. When I didn't have any means of transportation, when I didn't have my car, then I had to spend the night there because there was nowhere else I could go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's try another time. Please tell us the exact hours you worked. You started in the morning, after the 17th of May, picking up Dr. Stakic at his home. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That was about 6.30, that you could be at 7.00 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thereabouts. 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when would you bring Dr. Stakic regularly back to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we returned around 5.00, 6.00, 4.00, 3.00, depending on how long he was busy, because he didn't always have regular hours. He would stay longer. There were no working hours so that he would stay to work there longer, and I waited for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then when returning home to Omarska, you stayed with your car in Omarska until the next morning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Until that date, I left the car at my place, and I would pass by his house to fetch him, and then we would go on to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So was there any reason for you during this period of time to go back to Prijedor and to sleep in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that period of time, it did not happen that we went back and slept in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But on other occasions, you said "We went back Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and slept in Prijedor." It was, in fact, that both of you slept in Prijedor? Did Dr. Stakic also sleep in the building of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I slept. And that morning, Stakic also slept with me on that day, on the 30th. He was also with me. He also slept there. That night, that is the night that I spent there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And why was it that Dr. Stakic slept there on that day, together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know why, but we spent that night there. We were both in the municipal hall, and we slept there, and the janitor was there. And many others, we were quite a few there. Because we did not go back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were there any special plannings or other needs justifying to stay there and sleep there during this special night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't a special night. It just happened. It wasn't planned. We didn't go back, and I slept there, and he was there, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic going to any place where the incidents happened, say, Hambarine, Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Stakic didn't go with me to Hambarine, Kozarac. We didn't go to those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We heard a lot about places you haven't been following your testimony at all. May I ask the usher, therefore, to put on the ELMO, please, Exhibit S1. Let's turn the story the other way around. Looking on these small towns, hamlets, town of Prijedor, to the best of your recollection, where have you been together with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we mostly visited Prijedor, Kozarac, Lamovita, and Omarska. We passed that way all the time, except that day when we couldn't get through. This is the route that we used, Prijedor, Kozarusa, Kozarac, Babici, and Lamovita, Omarska. And then we went through Maricka and Cela on our way back the next day, via Cela, Maricka, and then back to Omarska. That would be the route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about all the other places, hamlets, small villages, you can see on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't go up there to Hambarine, Ostra Luka, no, I didn't. Tomasica, no I didn't go there. Maricka, yes. Gradina, I did go to. Now a little bit -- Brezicani, yes I have been there. Palanciste, yes, I have been there. And that's about it. Those are the places that I went to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the purpose of visiting Maricka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maricka, the purpose -- well, it wasn't a visit. We were returning via Petrovo and Cela, Tomasica, or Cela, Maricka, Omarska, when we couldn't get through, that was when we went on our way back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your testimony that the president of the Assembly didn't pay a visit to any other parts of the Prijedor Municipality together with you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With me, he didn't. He did not visit those other places with me. The places that I mentioned, yes, I went to them. I drove him to those places. Those others, no, I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic driving a Golf car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. A Golf? I didn't see him drive it. Perhaps privately, but I don't remember. He had a car - I don't know - before, but I don't know what he drove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever meet colleagues of yours, drivers of Autotransport Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see women -- first of all, women, men lining up in front of the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that I did see. I saw them queueing up there, standing, yes, as I came out of the municipal hall, I could see them standing in a queue in front of the police station. Yes, a hundred- or two-hundred-metre long queue. Yes, I did see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was the reason for these people queuing up in front of the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps they were being issued with some cards. I think they were being issued with some papers. I don't know what they were doing. I don't know. I know they were waiting for something in the queue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that you perfectly well knew, sir, that these people were queuing up to get a certificate that they could leave Prijedor Municipality together with their relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I know they were waiting for certificates of some sort, but I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sir, there's always a likelihood what persons do or don't. Is it really your testimony that you never discussed the question why these people were lining up in front of the SUP building together with Dr. Stakic? Did you never discuss this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no need for me to ask him that because I didn't want to address the conflict. I wasn't interested in that. I simply saw people in a long queue, and there was quite a crowd. So I saw what was happening, but I didn't want to ask. It was not necessary for me to ask about that. That wasn't mine, but I did see them waiting there. Yes, I did see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have the concrete page before me in the moment. But previously, you testified about a radical. Who was this radical person you mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned that with regard to the president, when you mentioned him and what he was. That's what I mentioned that. I don't know whether he was a member of the SDS or a radical. I believe that is when I said something about that, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was "radical" with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the difference is. I was not sure what the party was. I know that the word "radical" was mentioned, but I don't remember. I was not a member of any party. I only heard something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the moment, I don't have any further questions. The Defence is prepared for the line of questioning? Please, Mr. Lukic. Questioned by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stanar. My name is Branko Lukic. Together with John Ostojic, who is not with us today, and with Mr. Cirkovic, I represent Mr. Stakic's defence before this Tribunal. I will start from last things first. Judge Schomburg asked you about who is radical. Did you mean the party that he belonged to? Did you refer to the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a member of the Radical Party or the SDS or some other party. I never asked him what party he was a member of. And that's why I didn't know which party he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we make mention the word "Ljubija" and the word "Ljubljana" we understand what these two are all about. But for the Honourable Judges, can you tell us where Ljubljana is, in which republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljubljana is in Slovenia, and Ljubija is in Donja Ljubija. These are two totally different places. One is in Slovenia, and the other is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those are two different states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking about one morning, when you tried to go through Kozarac, and then -- was it on the way to work or from work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that evening, did you manage to go back home through Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't go back through Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that day on, is it true that you no longer could go through Kozarac on the way from Prijedor to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For three or five days, one couldn't go through Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am jumping from one subject to another to clarify some technical issues. You were asked about petrol vouchers or coupons. And you said that you received those from the cashier. Was that cashier somebody who had an office in the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had his office or she had her office in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember their names? You said that there were two persons involved in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were two persons involved, but I can't remember their names. I know who they were -- I know who they are now. Gordana Mijic [phoen] is one of them, and the other person is Stana [phoen]. But who they were at that time, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any case, at that time, you did not receive petrol vouchers from Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct, I didn't receive them from Slobodan Kuruzovic. We received them from Brezicani, and then we would take them to the petrol station, to Brezicani or the railway station. And when there was no petrol at the petrol stations, then we would go to the Brezicani warehouse or storage and we would obtain petrol from there if there was no petrol to be had from any of the petrol stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanar, when you were testifying about recruits being sent off to the army at the occasions that Dr. Stakic attended, amongst others, did you notice people from humanitarian institutions attending those send-offs and also there are women among them from Kovasavski Stija [phoen], for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were women and people like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just another clarification, if I may: In Smederevo, in Serbia, is there a huge iron works?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. That is the biggest iron works factory in Serbia. That's where rail wagons are made and other such things. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came across the barricades in Kevljani in the Kozarac region, was that a week or even before that time, even earlier, the attack on Prijedor, if you can remember? If you can't remember --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I did go that way, but I don't remember when that was. I'm not sure. And if I'm not sure, I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko. Further questions by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Stanar, today you stated - it's page 56, lines 11, 12 - "On several occasions, we had lunch in the restaurant when we were returning from Banja Luka." May I ask you to clarify, whom did you mean by saying "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President Stakic, and if vice-president was with him or the secretary, generally, and I was with them, and then we would stop for lunch and we would have lunch all of us together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On what occasions Dr. Stakic travelled to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he went to the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, when he went there or elsewhere, then he would stop by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How many times Dr. Stakic travelled to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was his driver, it may have been six or seven times that I took him to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what institutions Dr. Stakic visited in Banja Luka? Whom did he meet in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who he met with. I would take him to the municipal building. I would park the car there. He would enter the municipal building, and then I don't know who he met. I would usually sit in the car and wait for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And Dr. Stakic never explained to you why he is going to Banja Luka, whom he is going to meet, and what business he is going to perform in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was a driver, and it is not becoming a president to talk to a driver. And although we knew each other, he would never discuss official business with me. We would mostly chat, if anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was the strongest politician in 1992 in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not a politician, and I cannot answer that. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. Further questions by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that the authorities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina had offices in the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. As a matter of fact, I hear this for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as my colleague, John Ostojic, likes to say, with the Court's permission, but I forgot to ask two or three questions. They are not emanating from your questions and the Prosecutor's. Thank you. Further questions by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At one point, you stopped driving Dr. Stakic to Omarska. However, you continued living in Omarska, and you yourself travelled to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I continued commuting from Prijedor to Omarska every morning. I would go to Prijedor to work there. And I still do that. Every morning, I travel to Prijedor for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, could it happen that once you had already left for Omarska, that Dr. Stakic stayed in the municipal building or returned to it without you being aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On Saturdays, Sundays, for example, or after working hours, there was no way for me to know who was doing what. It would be the janitor who would know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any further questions? This is not the case. Then the witness is excused. Only a final question, to be correct, you were served the subpoena ducas tecum that you should bring along logbooks or similar records of the driving hours, the driving destinations. Did you try to get these, or weren't there any records? Would this be your testimony, that there was never a record taken about the destinations whom you would drive, at that time, no control at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, when I drove, there was no logbook. It was not recorded who was travelling where. We just had travel orders which said who was going where on what day. At the end of the month, we would hand over all of our travel orders to Zeljko Grahovac. So we did have our own orders. You maintained your records. We didn't record the names of the people we drove, but we did record the destinations. That is still the same. For example, today, we receive our orders, and then we fill out those orders with the destinations, be it Sarajevo, Belgrade, Banja Luka. Again, not the names of the persons that we drove. In the past, we didn't even enter the destinations where we drove to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but I can't understand this. You said in the past we didn't even enter the destinations where we drove to. So it would be just a piece of paper where you can read "order" by, and then nothing, nothing about the passenger, nothing would be the destination? What would be the sense of such document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a travel order valid for a month allowing you to move about, around Prijedor. This allowed you to travel all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if you are to go somewhere else, for example, to Croatia or to Belgrade, you need different travel orders. If you are in Prijedor, then you don't need any such thing. We had a piece of paper in which we recorded the number of kilometres that we did on that particular day, so we would enter the number of kilometres we started with, enter the number of kilometres we ended the day with, and we would sign that on every day, for every day. These were our -- these are our travel orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But just a moment ago, you stated: "We just had travel orders which said who was going where on what day. At the end of the month, we would hand over all our travel orders to Drago." So what's now correct? Did you have such travel orders which said who was going where on what day, or didn't you? Which part of your testimony is correct, the first or the second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both are correct. If you are in Prijedor and it's the vicinity, then we have monthly orders. If we travel somewhere else, then we have different orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then my question would be, why didn't you bring along these different orders where one could find the passengers and the destinations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know this would be necessary. But I can send all of those to you from the day when I started working. Actually, with the document on the day when I started working.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So these documents would be available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can send you the travel orders. However, I'm not sure whether I'll be able to find the travel orders from the year 1992 in the files. A lot of those documents have gone missing. I'm not sure whether they are still available. I can make some inquiries and see whether they are still available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Having received the court order, did you make any attempts to find these travel orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't have time to do that. I was away in Sarajevo for three days. I was in Brcko for two days. I came back on Saturday. At 11.00 on Saturday, I checked in, and then three days later, I left. So I really didn't have the time to do anything. I left in a bit of a hurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I can't see any additional questions. This concludes your testimony. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, what is the latest update? Has Mr. Kuruzovic already arrived so that he would be prepared to testify already tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have not had such information, so I think we're still on the information that he would arrive tomorrow and be ready to testify on Wednesday. But I can double-check and inform you during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the parties will be informed, because there was some rumour that he would already arrive today, and then we would take the opportunity and continue already tomorrow with the testimony of Mr. Kuruzovic in case the parties are prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are prepared, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're not prepared now, but hopefully by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. If it's possible, we should start with this tomorrow. We heard already the submissions on the rebuttal witnesses of the OTP. And then we heard no submission until now related to the, once again, requested for admission Donia report "Bosnia Krajina in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina." May I ask the Defence, what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you already know, our team divide our work, and that's in the purview of Mr. Ostojic's duties, and he'll be here with us tomorrow morning. So if it's not too late, I would ask you kindly to leave it until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's reasonable. So in any event, we will continue, but not tomorrow morning, tomorrow at 2.15 in Courtroom II. Because this week, we were -- we would sit tomorrow in Courtroom II in the afternoon; on Wednesday, in Courtroom I in the morning -- no, in Courtroom II in the morning; on Thursday, there would be a -- we would sit again in Courtroom II, and maybe once again on Friday, in Courtroom I in the afternoon. But things may change from hour to hour, let's wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Madam Registrar was kind enough and she provided us with the schedule. It was my mistake when I mentioned tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's no problem. And as I mentioned just a minute before, it might be that there are other changes due to overlapping cases in the moment. So are there any other issues to be discussed right now? Nothing from the Prosecution, nothing from the Defence. This concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
